The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has asked the Court of Appeal to overturn a judgement delivered by the Federal High Court on 5 November over the party’s leadership dispute, arguing that the trial court lacked the jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
The party has also filed an application seeking an injunction to restrain the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) from altering its leadership records or changing the nomination details of its presidential and governorship candidates pending the determination of the appeal.
In a statement issued on Tuesday by Phrank Shaibu, director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, the party said it had filed a Notice of Appeal containing 17 grounds challenging the judgement delivered by Justice Peter Lifu.
The ADC argued that the judgement was fundamentally flawed because the court allegedly lacked the authority to determine what it described as an internal leadership dispute.
It also faulted the court’s treatment of an earlier judgement of the Federal High Court delivered on 2 July on the party’s leadership transition, which it said remained valid and had not been set aside.
Mr Shaibu said the appeal questioned the trial court’s jurisdiction, the claimant’s legal standing, its assessment of disputed evidence, and the orders made against the party.
“The 17 grounds challenge the foundation, findings, and orders of Justice Lifu’s judgement. The ADC has asked the Court of Appeal to examine whether the trial court had jurisdiction, whether the claimant had standing, whether disputed evidence was properly assessed, and whether the sweeping orders made against the party can stand in law,” he said.

The party is also challenging an earlier ruling delivered on 24 July, which allowed Nafiu Gombe to amend his originating summons despite the ADC’s outstanding objection to the trial court’s jurisdiction.
In a separate appellant’s brief, the party argued that the trial court should have determined its preliminary objection on jurisdiction before granting Mr Gombe permission to amend his suit.
According to the ADC, the proposed amendment changed the description of parties and the capacity in which a defendant was sued without obtaining the required leave of court.
The brief, settled by J.S. Okutepa, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), asked the Court of Appeal to set aside the amendment order and determine the party’s outstanding jurisdictional objection.
The ADC further argued that Mr Lifu delivered the 5 November judgement based on an amended court process that was already under appeal, without waiting for the appellate court to resolve the challenge.
Beyond seeking to overturn the judgement, the ADC says it wants the Court of Appeal to prevent INEC from acting on it while the legal challenge remains pending.
The party is asking the court to restrain the electoral commission from changing its leadership records or interfering with the names and nomination particulars of its presidential and governorship candidates.
It argued that allowing INEC to implement the judgement before the appeal is determined could create changes that may be difficult to reverse, even if the appellate court eventually rules in its favour.
The party therefore wants the Court of Appeal to preserve the status quo that existed before the 5 November judgement to prevent the appeal from being rendered ineffective.
Mr Shaibu warned that any changes to the party’s records or candidates while the applications remain pending could prejudice the outcome of the legal proceedings.
“INEC must not make changes that could pre-empt the court’s decision or put the party’s candidates in jeopardy while our applications are pending,” he said.
He added that the party would continue to pursue its legal challenge and defend its leadership and its members’ decisions in court.
The leadership crisis in the ADC followed the resignation of Ralph Nwosu as the party’s national chairman and the emergence of former Senate President David Mark as his successor, with Rauf Aregbesola becoming national secretary.
However, Mr Gombe, a former deputy national chairman of the party, challenged the leadership transition, claiming that he was entitled to succeed Mr Nwosu. The disagreement later led to a series of court cases over the legitimacy of the Mark-led leadership.
On 2 July, the Federal High Court delivered an earlier judgement on the leadership transition.
However, the dispute resurfaced after Mr Lifu’s judgement of 5 November, which nullified the processes that produced the Mark-led leadership and affected decisions the party had taken, including its preparations for the 2027 elections.
The ADC rejected the ruling and vowed to challenge it in court.
